source.title: When the Preconditioning Exponent Turns Negative: Learning-Rate Coupling and Cross-Environment Generalization

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. No garbling or cutoff affecting the reported results is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports optimizer and cross-environment generalization results, but evaluates a synthetic environmental shift rather than same-distribution generalization on natural labels. The prompt explicitly treats out-of-distribution generalization as separate.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure the train–test gap or test any listed version in its stated setting. Its optimizer and feature-allocation results concern cross-environment accuracy on synthetic data, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The main numerical results are in Tables 1–5; cited prior-work findings are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures optimizer-dependent feature allocation and accuracy under synthetic environmental shifts using one affine classifier. It does not test any listed version. In particular, it does not compare adaptive methods with SGD on the image or language benchmarks named in V4; its p=0 update is momentum-like, and the recorded results are oracle-selected cross-environment accuracies.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. In this single-seed, finite-budget synthetic study, the cross-environment-optimal exponent decreases with learning rate and becomes negative at high learning rates, while source validation still selects positive exponents. Lower exponents reduce relative spurious and noise allocation. The authors explicitly reject a universal optimizer-improvement claim.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic paired environmental-shift experiment with a single affine classifier and a p × learning-rate sweep; it does not reproduce the natural-data, same-distribution evaluations in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported cross-environment-optimal exponent changes with learning rate and source environment; source-validation and robust selection criteria select different exponents. The paper reports one seed and fixed batch size 128.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 4 reports mean cross-environment accuracy at an exponent selected retrospectively using target test accuracy, ranging from 83.44% to 98.14% across source environments and learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oracle-selected cross-environment performance depends on learning rate and source environment in this synthetic affine-classifier experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 1 and 4 show that the cross-environment-optimal exponent decreases with log10 learning rate, with fitted slopes −0.270 to −0.300 and R² 0.972–0.996. Table 2 shows positive source-validation optima and negative robust optima at learning rate 0.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The useful preconditioning exponent depends jointly on learning rate and whether selection targets source validation or environmental robustness.

record.problems: One random seed, one affine classifier, synthetic data, and a fixed 50-epoch budget; 92.38% of runs select the final-epoch checkpoint. Reported accuracy differences are described as single-seed mechanism magnitudes, not confidence intervals. Robust criteria use target test environments for retrospective oracle analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 provide additional selected-exponent and best-negative-versus-best-nonnegative comparisons; Table 5 reports source-selected cross-environment accuracies. These were omitted because they remain out-of-distribution findings and the core sweep results are already represented in rows r1–r20. Feature-allocation and margin-decomposition plots are not extracted as rows because their plotted numerical values are not fully stated in text, except selected ratios described in Section 5.4.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe; chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD performance on image or language benchmarks under limited or broader tuning, including weight decay and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes that recover performance.
Dropout effects, dependence on training-set size and dropout strength, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The exclusion rests on the specific constructs and comparisons in V1–V8, not a blanket requirement that every version measure a train–test gap. The accuracy rows do not themselves record the selected exponents or establish the fitted exponent trend; that finding comes from Tables 1, 2 and 4. Single-seed results provide no estimate of between-seed uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside generalization on natural labels; the paper uses neither random labels nor natural data.
Width sweep past interpolation on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures on image datasets.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons on image-classification or language benchmarks, including tuning breadth and same-distribution held-out performance.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or comparisons with norm- and margin-based generalization measures.
Removing influential memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
